488: The variety and product interaction was non-significant for this character.
490: The most probable basis of the higher texture scores of the fortified treatments is that the panel preferred a softer, less chewy and more readily broken product, and the instrumental determinations confirm that fortification produced precisely that character (Bourne, 2002; Szczesniak, 2002). Consumers of idli expect a soft, spongy crumb, and the dilution of the starch and protein network by the vegetable extract, together with the moisture it contributes, conferred exactly that quality (Reddy et al., 1981; Nisha et al., 2005; Durgadevi and Shetty, 2012). The close agreement between the instrumental values and the panel scores supports the position of Rosenthal (1999), Wilkinson et al. (2000) and Szczesniak (2002) that texture profile analysis of a steamed cereal product predicts perceived texture reliably, and it entails that the instrumental determination may be employed to screen new formulations in advance of sensory evaluation.
499: Appearance score (Table 4.40 and Fig. 4.40) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KBI (8.89), followed by RBI (8.49), and lowest in DI (6.39). Among the products the mean value was 8.31 in the beet fortified product, 8.06 in the carrot fortified product and 7.24 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (8.43) and lowest in Dudeshwar (7.27).
500: The variety and product interaction was non-significant for this character.
502: The most probable basis of the very high appearance scores of the fortified treatments is the introduction of an attractive natural colour into what is otherwise a plain white product. The colour difference recorded for every fortified treatment lay many times above the threshold at which a change becomes visible, so that the difference in appearance was immediately apparent to the panel (Francis, 1995; Hutchings, 1999; Pathare et al., 2013). Consumers respond positively to natural pigments in traditional foods, particularly where the colour is recognisably derived from a familiar vegetable rather than from a synthetic additive (Delgado-Vargas et al., 2000; Stintzing and Carle, 2004; Chhikara et al., 2019). Comparable improvements in the appearance rating of traditional Indian foods following the addition of pigment-rich fractions have been reported by Pal et al. (2019) and Bagchi et al. (2020).
511: Cooking quality score (Table 4.41 and Fig. 4.41) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KBI (8.44), followed by RBI (8.04), and lowest in DI (5.94). Among the products the mean value was 7.86 in the beet fortified product, 7.61 in the carrot fortified product and 6.79 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (7.98) and lowest in Dudeshwar (6.82).
512: The variety and product interaction was non-significant for this character.
514: Cooking quality as judged by the panel encompasses the shape, surface finish and uniformity of the steamed product, and the most probable basis of the higher scores of the fortified treatments is that the added moisture and fibre improved the flow of the batter and permitted it to spread evenly within the mould (Reddy et al., 1981; Nisha et al., 2005; Durgadevi and Shetty, 2012). A batter of suitable consistency retains the gas generated during fermentation more evenly and yields a product of regular shape and smooth surface (Mukherjee et al., 1965; Soni and Sandhu, 1990; Sridevi et al., 2010). The uniform colour of the fortified products may have contributed indirectly, since surface irregularities are less conspicuous against a coloured background than against a white one (Hutchings, 1999; Pathare et al., 2013).
523: Overall acceptability score (Table 4.42 and Fig. 4.42) differed significantly among the twelve treatment combinations. It was highest in KBI (8.64), followed by RBI (8.24), and lowest in DI (6.14). Among the products the mean value was 8.06 in the beet fortified product, 7.82 in the carrot fortified product and 6.99 in the plain product. Among the varieties it was highest in Kalojira (8.19) and lowest in Dudeshwar (7.02).
524: The variety and product interaction was non-significant for this character.
526: Overall acceptability constitutes a composite judgement, and the most probable basis of the ranking obtained is that the fortified treatments were superior for the three attributes weighing most heavily within it, namely appearance, texture and taste (Amerine et al., 1965; Meilgaard et al., 2007). The natural pigment rendered the product visually attractive, the dilution of the starch and protein network rendered it softer and more readily eaten, and the free sugars of the extract improved its taste (Reddy et al., 1981; Sharma et al., 2012; Pathare et al., 2013; Chhikara et al., 2019). The small loss of rice aroma did not offset these gains, which is consistent with the finding that aroma alone was uncorrelated with acceptability in the present data. The non-significant interaction constitutes an important practical result, since it demonstrates that the advantage conferred by fortification was of equal magnitude in every variety and is therefore a general property of the treatment rather than of any one landrace, a conclusion consonant with the reports of Pal et al. (2019) and Bagchi et al. (2020) on pigment-enriched traditional Indian foods.
529: The relations among the forty two quality parameters were examined by computing the Pearson correlation coefficient over twenty four treatment means, namely the twelve treatment combinations in each of the two years. The full matrix is presented as a heat map in Fig. 4.43 and the correlation of overall acceptability with every other parameter in Table 4.43. At twenty two degrees of freedom the coefficient must exceed 0.404 to attain significance at the 5 per cent level and 0.515 at the 1 per cent level (Snedecor and Cochran, 1994). It should be borne in mind throughout that a correlation establishes only that two characters covaried within this data set; it does not of itself demonstrate that one caused the other.
535: The three bioactive fractions were very closely associated. Total phenol correlated with total flavonoid (r = 0.983) and with total antioxidant activity (r = 0.971), and total flavonoid with total antioxidant activity (r = 0.945), all three coefficients being significant at the 1 per cent level. Coefficients of this magnitude are unsurprising, since the three assays determine the same group of compounds: the DPPH assay records the hydrogen-donating power of the phenolic and flavonoid pool, so that its value must follow that pool, as has likewise been reported for rice by Goufo and Trindade (2014) and for idli by Kaviyaselvan et al. (2026). Total soluble protein correlated with total phenol (r = 0.767) and phytate with total phenol (r = 0.632). These two associations have a different basis, namely that protein, phytate and bound phenolic acids co-occur in the aleurone and sub-aleurone layers of the grain, so that a treatment raising one tends to raise the others.
536: The carbohydrate fractions were negatively associated with the bioactive fractions throughout. Total carbohydrate was negatively correlated with total phenol (r = -0.913) and starch with total antioxidant activity (r = -0.955). Total carbohydrate was itself correlated with starch (r = 0.895) and amylose (r = 0.824), and lightness with yellowness (r = 0.995) and with total carbohydrate (r = 0.832). This entire block of coefficients expresses a single gradient rather than several separate effects: each gram of vegetable extract added to the batter displaces a gram of rice and black gram, so that starch is removed and pigment added in the same operation (Chhikara et al., 2019). The fortified products were therefore darker, lower in starch and richer in antioxidants concurrently, and lightness moved with total carbohydrate because the pale colour of the plain product derives from its undiluted starch matrix (Pathare et al., 2013).
537: Several of the textural coefficients are mechanical rather than biological in origin. Hardness correlated with gumminess (r = 0.913) and chewiness (r = 0.816), which follows from both being computed from hardness and cohesiveness rather than determined directly (Bourne, 2002). Springiness correlated with amylose (r = 0.640) and cohesiveness with amylose (r = 0.484), amylose forming the gel that permits the crumb to recover after compression, so that a product of higher amylose content is firmer and more elastic (Tester et al., 2004). Resistant starch was negatively correlated with the predicted glycaemic index (r = -0.587), as is to be expected since resistant starch is the fraction escaping digestion. Ash correlated with calcium (r = 0.804), which demonstrates that the mineral load of the product was governed largely by the calcium supplied by beetroot.
538: The coefficients obtained for overall acceptability indicate what the panel in fact responded to. It was negatively correlated with total carbohydrate (r = -0.895), non-resistant starch (r = -0.716), starch (r = -0.710), springiness (r = -0.691) and lightness (r = -0.662), and positively correlated with total flavonoid (r = 0.782), total antioxidant activity (r = 0.780), total phenol (r = 0.773), hue angle (r = 0.762), phytate (r = 0.753) and total soluble protein (r = 0.746). The panel accordingly awarded low scores to products that were starchy, springy and pale, and high scores to products that were coloured and pigment-rich, which is the profile of the fortified treatments. The probable reason is that colour and tenderness determine the acceptability of a steamed cereal food to a greater extent than any single chemical constituent (Pathare et al., 2013; Kaviyaselvan et al., 2026). The positive coefficients for phytate and total soluble protein should not be construed as causal, since these constituents simply rose in the same treatments that were fortified and therefore covaried with acceptability without influencing it. Aroma was the sole sensory attribute uncorrelated with acceptability (r = -0.123), most probably because aroma derives from the 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline of the rice whereas acceptability was determined by colour and texture.
539: One feature of the matrix requires comment. Taste, flavour, texture, appearance, cooking quality and overall acceptability were correlated with one another at exactly unity, the six scores differing only by a constant. This is a property of the manner in which the scores were recorded and not a biological finding. Their relations with the physico-chemical parameters are therefore identical, and only overall acceptability has been carried forward into the multivariate analyses that follow.
542: Principal component analysis was performed on the standardised values of the forty two parameters over the twenty four treatment means. The method takes a large number of related parameters and derives a few new axes carrying most of the variation, each axis constituting a weighted combination of the original parameters. The weights are termed loadings, a high loading denoting that the parameter contributes strongly to that axis (Jolliffe, 2002). Only components with an eigenvalue above unity were retained, which is the customary practice for food quality data in which many related characters are determined on the same samples (Granato et al., 2018). The eigenvalues are given in Table 4.44, the scree plot in Fig. 4.44, the loadings in Table 4.45 and the biplot of the first two components in Fig. 4.45.
553: Seven components returned eigenvalues above unity. The first component explained 50.12 per cent of the total variation and the second 14.12 per cent, the two together accounting for 64.24 per cent and the first five components for 86.66 per cent. A first component of this magnitude demonstrates that one principal effect runs through the entire data set rather than several independent effects.
554: The loadings identify that effect. The positive pole of the first component was defined by total antioxidant activity (1.005), total phenol (0.968), total flavonoid (0.942), total soluble sugar (0.905) and overall acceptability (0.874), and the negative pole by total carbohydrate (-0.988), non-resistant starch (-0.965), starch (-0.963), lightness (-0.927), yellowness (-0.893), chroma (-0.888), springiness (-0.875) and amylose (-0.836). This is the same dilution gradient evident in the correlation matrix, since the addition of a vegetable extract removes starch and adds pigment in a single operation, so that all these parameters must move together in a fixed pattern (Chhikara et al., 2019). The first component may therefore be designated a fortification axis. A single dominant component of this kind is common in fortified and fermented cereal products, in which one processing step alters many characters simultaneously (Granato et al., 2018).
555: The second component carried a considerably smaller share of the variation. Its positive pole was defined by total protein (0.922), aroma (0.658), manganese (0.617), gumminess (0.608) and hardness (0.592), and its negative pole by resistant starch (-0.783), beta-carotene (-0.644) and total colour difference (-0.590). This axis separates the carrot fortified treatments from the remainder. The probable reason is that the two fortifying materials behave differently: carrot supplies carotenoid and dietary fibre but very little free sugar, so that it raises beta-carotene and resistant starch and leaves the product firmer, whereas beetroot supplies free sugar and betalain instead (Sharma et al., 2012). The second component therefore describes the difference between the two vegetables rather than any difference between the varieties.
